items.q: You write `import json` and it works without installing anything. Why?
options: You must have installed it earlier without noticing
json was downloaded automatically from the internet
json is part of Python's standard library, which ships with the interpreter — no install needed

explain.right: The standard library (json, datetime, os, ...) comes bundled with Python, so those modules import directly.
explain.wrong: It isn't fetched on the fly, and not every module is built in — third-party ones need pip install first.

items.q: `import requests` raises `ModuleNotFoundError`. What's the most likely fix?
options: Run `pip install requests` in the terminal — requests is a third-party package, not part of the standard library

explain.right: requests is third-party, so it must be installed with pip (ideally into your project's venv) before you can import it.
explain.wrong: Restarting, renaming, or assigning a variable won't make an uninstalled package importable.

items.q: What problem does a virtual environment (venv) solve?
options: It gives each project its own private set of packages, so projects needing different versions don't clash
It connects your code to the internet

explain.right: A venv isolates a project's packages so one project's versions never break another's — the cure for shared, conflicting installs.
explain.wrong: A venv doesn't affect speed, networking, or testing; its whole job is per-project isolation.

items.q: You save your own script as `json.py` and then `import json`. What's the likely problem?
options: Python may import YOUR file instead of the standard-library json, breaking json.dumps and friends

explain.right: Python searches the current directory first, so a file named json.py can shadow the real module; never name files after modules you import.
explain.wrong: Filenames do matter for imports, nothing is deleted, and the breakage shows up when you use the module, not always at import.
